s: Under which constitutional provision may Parliament legislate on a matter in the State List when it is necessary in the national interest?
x: Article 249 enables Parliament to legislate on State List matters in the national interest, subject to a resolution of the Rajya Sabha supported by the prescribed majority.
tq: Use the article-condition pair to distinguish the special legislative powers.
sec: Parliament legislating on State List → article and condition  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. National interest — Article 249
2. National Emergency — Article 250
3. Request of two or more States — Article 252
4. International agreements — Article 253
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
x: All four pairs are correctly matched. Articles 249, 250, 252 and 253 respectively concern national interest, Emergency, State resolutions and international agreements.
tq: Start from the sure article-condition pairs and eliminate codes containing a wrong pairing.
sec: Parliament legislating on State List → article and condition  [APPSC]

s: Parliament may legislate on a State List subject under Article 250 when:
o: the President receives an international treaty
a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation
the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution in the national interest
two or more State Legislatures request it
x: Article 250 operates while a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation and permits Parliament to make laws on State List matters.
tq: Identify the triggering condition rather than recalling the article number alone.
sec: Parliament legislating on State List → article and condition  [APPSC]

s:
With reference to Article 252, consider the following statements:
1. The legislatures of two or more States must pass resolutions requesting parliamentary legislation.
2. Any other State may adopt the resulting law later by passing a resolution of its legislature.
3. The requesting State Legislatures may independently repeal the law enacted by Parliament.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false: only Parliament can amend or repeal a law enacted under Article 252.
tq: Find the statement that assigns legislative power to the wrong authority.
sec: Parliament legislating on State List → article and condition  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following is NOT an example of legislation enacted under Article 252?
o: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
x: The Prize Competition Act, 1955, Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 and Water Act, 1974 are examples associated with Article 252. The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 is not included in the listed examples.
tq: Find the option outside the specified group of Article 252 examples.
sec: Parliament legislating on State List → article and condition  [APPSC]

s:
Which of the following Acts is associated with parliamentary legislation under Article 252?
1. Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976
2. Transplantation of Human Organs Act, 1994
3. Prize Competition Act, 1955
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: All three Acts are listed as examples of laws enacted by Parliament under Article 252 following resolutions by two or more State Legislatures.
tq: Test the complete list by checking whether each named example belongs to the same constitutional route.
sec: Parliament legislating on State List → article and condition  [APPSC]

s: Under Article 356, legislation for a State during President’s Rule may be made by:
o: Parliament, or the President under delegated authority
the Governor alone without constitutional authority
x: During President’s Rule, Parliament may legislate for the State; the President may also exercise this legislative function when Parliament delegates it.
tq: Apply the ‘who would do this job?’ method to distinguish the competent authority.
sec: Parliament legislating on State List → article and condition  [APPSC]

s: A law made for a State during President’s Rule continues after the Proclamation ends until:
o: the State Legislature alters, repeals or re-enacts it
the Supreme Court declares it permanent
the Governor issues an ordinance replacing it
x: Such a law does not automatically lapse when President’s Rule ends. It continues until the State Legislature alters, repeals or re-enacts it.
tq: Test the post-emergency effect instead of confusing continuation with automatic repeal.
sec: Parliament legislating on State List → article and condition  [APPSC]

s: Which Article empowers Parliament to make laws for the whole or any part of India to implement treaties, agreements and conventions?
x: Article 253 empowers Parliament to legislate for the whole or any part of India for implementing treaties, agreements and conventions.
tq: Match the international-law purpose with its specific constitutional provision.
sec: Parliament legislating on State List → article and condition  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the effect of a Parliamentary law made under Article 249 or Article 250 when it conflicts with a State law?
o: The Governor decides which law will prevail.
The Parliamentary law prevails over the State law.
The State law prevails because State subjects remain exclusively State matters.
Both laws become void to the extent of conflict.
x: Article 251 provides that a Parliamentary law made under Article 249 or 250 prevails over an inconsistent State law.
tq: Use the conflict rule to identify the superior law and reject the wrong authority.
sec: Parliament legislating on State List → article and condition  [APPSC]

s: The resolution authorising Parliament to legislate on a State List matter in the national interest is passed by:
o: the Rajya Sabha by two-thirds of members present and voting
the Rajya Sabha by a majority of the total membership
the Lok Sabha by a simple majority
both Houses by a special majority
x: Article 249 requires a resolution of the Rajya Sabha supported by two-thirds of the members present and voting. The Lok Sabha does not participate in passing this resolution.
tq: Separate the required House from the exact form of majority.
sec: Article 249 resolution - Rajya Sabha majority, duration, extension  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements regarding a resolution under Article 249:
1. It remains in force for a period not exceeding one year.
2. It may be renewed any number of times.
3. Each renewal may extend it for a period exceeding one year.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false: every renewal can extend the resolution only for one year at a time.
tq: Watch the limiting phrase ‘one year at a time’ in a duration question.
sec: Article 249 resolution - Rajya Sabha majority, duration, extension  [APPSC]

s: A resolution of the Rajya Sabha under Article 249 can be renewed:
o: any number of times, one year at a time
indefinitely without a fixed renewal period
only twice for one year each
x: The resolution may be renewed any number of times, but each renewal is limited to one year.
tq: Distinguish unlimited renewals from an unlimited duration for each renewal.
sec: Article 249 resolution - Rajya Sabha majority, duration, extension  [APPSC]

s: A law made by Parliament under Article 249 ceases to have effect:
o: six months before the resolution lapses
only when the State Legislature passes a contrary law
immediately when the Rajya Sabha resolution lapses
six months after the resolution lapses
x: A law enacted under Article 249 continues for six months after the resolution authorising it lapses, after which it ceases to operate.
tq: Focus on the delayed legal effect rather than the date on which the enabling resolution ends.
sec: Article 249 resolution - Rajya Sabha majority, duration, extension  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following statements regarding State legislative power during the operation of Article 249 is correct?
o: The State Legislature may legislate only after obtaining the consent of the Rajya Sabha.
The State Legislature’s power is suspended, but the Governor may legislate.
The State Legislature may still legislate, but the Parliamentary law prevails in case of conflict.
The State Legislature is dissolved for the entire duration of the resolution.
x: An Article 249 resolution does not suspend the State Legislature’s power. However, the Parliamentary law prevails if it conflicts with a State law.
tq: Reject the extreme claim that a special Union power automatically removes State legislative power.
sec: Article 249 resolution - Rajya Sabha majority, duration, extension  [APPSC]

s: During a Proclamation of Emergency, which one of the following is constitutionally correct?
o: The Prime Minister alone may legislate on State List matters.
Only the President may enact ordinary laws on State List matters.
Parliament may legislate on State List matters for the whole or any part of India.
The State Legislature loses all legislative powers permanently.
x: Article 250 permits Parliament to legislate on State List matters for the whole or any part of India while the Emergency is in operation.
tq: Identify the constitutional law-making body instead of a minister or individual executive authority.
sec: Parliament legislating on State List → article and condition  [APPSC]

s: Laws made by Parliament under Article 250 become inoperative:
o: three months after the Emergency ends
six months after the Emergency ends
one year after the Emergency ends
immediately on the withdrawal of the Emergency
x: A law made under Article 250 becomes inoperative six months after the Proclamation of Emergency ceases to operate.
tq: Distinguish the six-month post-Emergency period from the duration of the Emergency itself.
sec: Parliament legislating on State List → article and condition  [APPSC]

s:
Arrange the following provisions in chronological order of their Article numbers:
A. Legislation in national interest
B. Legislation during National Emergency
C. Legislation on request of two or more States
D. Legislation for implementing international agreements
x: The provisions correspond respectively to Articles 249, 250, 252 and 253. Therefore, the correct order is A, B, C, D.
tq: Convert each description into its article number and then arrange the numbers.
sec: Parliament legislating on State List → article and condition  [APPSC]

s: Under Article 246, the power of Parliament to make laws is exclusive in respect of matters contained in:
o: List I of the Seventh Schedule
List II of the Seventh Schedule
List III of the Seventh Schedule
x: Article 246(1) gives Parliament exclusive power over matters in the Union List, or List I, subject to the constitutional provisions.
tq: Match each clause of Article 246 with the corresponding legislative list.
sec: Conflict between lists - Article 246, order of precedence  [APPSC]

s:
Which of the following statements correctly reflects Article 246?
1. Parliament has exclusive power over List I.
2. Parliament and State Legislatures can both legislate over List III.
3. State Legislatures have power over List II, subject to Parliament’s powers under Article 246(1) and 246(2).
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: All three statements correctly describe Articles 246(1), 246(2) and 246(3), respectively.
tq: Check each sub-clause separately before selecting the coded combination.
sec: Conflict between lists - Article 246, order of precedence  [APPSC]

s: A law made by a State Legislature under the State List conflicts with a valid law made by Parliament under the Concurrent List. Which law ordinarily prevails?
o: The Parliamentary law, because the Concurrent List has precedence over the State List
The later law, irrespective of the legislative body
The law approved by the Governor
The State law, because the subject is administered by the State
x: The Concurrent List has precedence over the State List. Therefore, a valid Parliamentary law on a Concurrent List matter ordinarily prevails over an inconsistent State law.
tq: Apply the order of precedence to a concrete conflict rather than relying on administrative control.
sec: Conflict between lists - Article 246, order of precedence  [APPSC]

s: Under Article 246(4), Parliament may make laws on any matter for:
o: areas not included in a State, such as Union Territories
only the States included in List II
only areas declared by the Supreme Court
x: Article 246(4) enables Parliament to legislate on any matter for any part of the territory of India not included in a State, including Union Territories.
tq: Use the territorial exception in Article 246(4) to identify the correct scope.
sec: Conflict between lists - Article 246, order of precedence  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 246(4):
1. Parliament may legislate for Union Territories on matters in all three Lists.
2. The legislative power of Parliament for Union Territories is confined to the Union List.
3. The provision applies to areas not included in a State.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false because Parliament’s power for Union Territories extends to all three Lists, not merely the Union List.
tq: Spot the restrictive word ‘confined’ and compare it with the wider territorial power.
sec: Conflict between lists - Article 246, order of precedence  [APPSC]

s: With reference to Article 246A, which one of the following is correct regarding Goods and Services Tax legislation?
o: Parliament and State Legislatures have no power over GST without a Rajya Sabha resolution.
Only Parliament can make GST laws, including laws on intra-State supply.
Only State Legislatures can make GST laws.
Both Parliament and State Legislatures can make GST laws, but Parliament has exclusive power over inter-State supply.
x: Article 246A gives both Parliament and State Legislatures power to make GST laws. Parliament has exclusive power regarding GST on inter-State supplies, including IGST matters.
tq: Separate the shared GST power from Parliament’s exclusive inter-State competence.
sec: Conflict between lists - Article 246, order of precedence  [APPSC]

s: Article 246A was inserted by which Constitutional Amendment Act?
x: Article 246A was introduced by the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, which established the constitutional framework for GST.
tq: Match the distinctive constitutional article with the amendment that introduced it.
sec: Conflict between lists - Article 246, order of precedence  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following statements is NOT correct regarding the five constitutional situations in which Parliament may legislate on State List matters?
o: Article 252 operates when one State Legislature alone requests parliamentary legislation.
Article 356 operates during President’s Rule in a State.
Article 250 operates during a Proclamation of Emergency.
x: Article 252 requires resolutions from the legislatures of two or more States, not one State Legislature alone. Articles 249, 250 and 356 are correctly described.
tq: Test the minimum numerical condition and reject the deceptively shortened requirement.
sec: Parliament legislating on State List → article and condition  [APPSC]

s: A State Bill providing for compulsory acquisition of property is required to be:
o: Certified by the Speaker before introduction
Reserved by the Governor for the President
x: Bills providing for compulsory acquisition of property are among the Bills that must be reserved by the Governor for the President's consideration.
tq: Apply the mandatory-reservation rule to a concrete legislative situation.
sec: Centre's control over state legislation - bills needing President's sanction, reservation

s: Taxes on water or electricity in an inter-State river project require reservation of the State Bill under which constitutional provision?
x: Article 288 concerns taxes on water or electricity in relation to certain inter-State river projects, and Bills imposing such taxes must be reserved as specified.
tq: Use article-number discrimination among closely related provisions.
sec: Centre's control over state legislation - bills needing President's sanction, reservation

s: The previous sanction of the President is required before introducing a State Bill imposing restrictions on trade, commerce or intercourse under:
x: Article 304(b) requires the previous sanction of the President before introduction of a State Bill imposing reasonable restrictions on inter-State trade, commerce or intercourse.
tq: Distinguish previous sanction before introduction from reservation after passage.
sec: Centre's control over state legislation - bills needing President's sanction, reservation

s: Under Article 201, the President in relation to a Bill reserved by the Governor may:
o: Return every Bill, including a Money Bill, for reconsideration
Direct reconsideration of a non-Money Bill, but is not bound to assent after reconsideration
Only withhold assent and has no power to direct reconsideration
Transfer the Bill to the Supreme Court for final approval
x: The President has an absolute veto over a reserved State Bill, and may direct return of a non-Money Bill for reconsideration. Even after reconsideration, the President is not bound to give assent.
tq: Separate the President's return power from the binding effect of reconsideration.
sec: Centre's control over state legislation - bills needing President's sanction, reservation

s:
Consider the following statements regarding the 2025 Presidential Reference on gubernatorial assent to Bills:
1. It rejected rigid constitutional deadlines for the Governor.
2. It recognised deemed assent merely because the Governor had not acted within a judicially fixed period.
3. It stated that action should be taken as soon as possible.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: The November 2025 Presidential Reference opinion rejected rigid deadlines and deemed assent, while requiring action as soon as possible. Therefore, statements 1 and 3 are correct.
tq: Catch the reversal between rigid timelines and the constitutional standard of prompt action.
sec: Centre's control over state legislation - bills needing President's sanction, reservation

s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the Presidential Reference opinion of November 2025 from the ruling in State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu dated 8 April 2025?
o: The ruling concerned Article 248, whereas the Reference concerned Article 254.
The Reference rejected rigid deadlines and deemed assent, whereas the ruling prescribed timelines including deemed assent.
The Reference accepted deemed assent, whereas the ruling rejected it.
Both decisions prescribed identical rigid deadlines.
x: The 8 April 2025 ruling prescribed timelines and recognised deemed assent, while the November 2025 Presidential Reference opinion rejected rigid deadlines and deemed assent.
tq: Discriminate between two closely dated decisions by comparing their holdings.
sec: Centre's control over state legislation - bills needing President's sanction, reservation

s: In State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu, decided on 8 April 2025, which timeline was associated with the Governor's action on Bills?
o: Two months, three months and two months on re-passage
Three months, six months and three months on re-passage
One month, three months and one month on re-passage
One month, six months and one month on re-passage
x: The ruling referred to timelines of one month, three months and one month on re-passage, along with the concept of deemed assent.
tq: Retain the three-part timeline as a numerical sequence rather than relying on general impressions.
sec: Centre's control over state legislation - bills needing President's sanction, reservation

s: Which of the following propositions is associated with the November 2025 opinion on the Presidential Reference under Article 143?
o: The Governor must act within a rigid judicially prescribed period in every case.
The merits of the Governor's decision are always justiciable.
Only limited mandamus may issue for prolonged unexplained inaction.
Article 142 can substitute the constitutional functions of the Governor and President.
x: The opinion held that Article 142 cannot substitute the Governor or President, merits are not generally justiciable, and only limited mandamus may be issued for prolonged unexplained inaction.
tq: Identify the carefully qualified judicial remedy instead of an absolute proposition.
sec: Centre's control over state legislation - bills needing President's sanction, reservation

s: Which constitutional provision vests residuary legislative power in Parliament?
x: Article 248 vests residuary legislative power in Parliament, including the power to legislate on residuary matters of taxation.
tq: Directly identify the article associated with residuary legislative competence.
sec: Residuary legislative power - Article 248, Part XI, Union List Entry 97

s: Residuary legislative matters are associated with which entry of the Union List?
x: Union List Entry 97, read with Article 248, covers matters not enumerated in the State List or Concurrent List, including residuary taxation.
tq: Use the exact entry number to distinguish residuary power from neighbouring Union List entries.
sec: Residuary legislative power - Article 248, Part XI, Union List Entry 97

s: Article 248 is located in which Part of the Constitution?
x: Article 248 is located in Part XI, which deals with relations between the Union and the States and extends from Articles 245 to 263.
tq: Match the article with its constitutional Part, not merely with its subject.
sec: Residuary legislative power - Article 248, Part XI, Union List Entry 97

s:
Which of the following are covered by Parliament's residuary legislative power under Article 248 read with Entry 97 of the Union List?
1. Matters not enumerated in the State List.
2. Matters not enumerated in the Concurrent List.
3. Residuary taxation.
Select the correct answer using the code below.
x: Parliament has exclusive power over matters not listed in the State or Concurrent Lists, and this power includes residuary taxation.
tq: Choose the comprehensive option when all components of the constitutional rule are present.
sec: Residuary legislative power - Article 248, Part XI, Union List Entry 97

s: The constitutional arrangement relating to residuary powers in India was borrowed from:
x: The idea of vesting residuary powers in the central legislature was borrowed from Canada, a federation with a strong Centre.
tq: Test the comparative constitutional source of a federal feature.
sec: Residuary legislative power - Article 248, Part XI, Union List Entry 97

s: Which one of the following correctly states the present and original number of subjects in the Union and Concurrent Lists respectively?
o: Union 98 originally and 97 today; Concurrent 52 originally and 47 today
Union 97 originally and 98 today; Concurrent 47 originally and 52 today
Union 97 originally and 98 today; Concurrent 52 originally and 47 today
Union 98 originally and 100 today; Concurrent 47 originally and 52 today
x: The Union List has 98 subjects today compared with 97 originally, while the Concurrent List has 52 today compared with 47 originally.
tq: Compare present figures with original figures in the correct order of the two Lists.
sec: Residuary legislative power - Article 248, Part XI, Union List Entry 97

s: What did the Sarkaria Commission recommend regarding residuary powers, apart from taxation?
o: Giving residuary taxation exclusively to the States
Moving all residuary powers except taxation to the Concurrent List
Transferring all residuary powers to the State List
x: The Sarkaria Commission in 1988 recommended moving all residuary powers other than taxation to the Concurrent List.
tq: Identify the precise exception in a commission recommendation.
sec: Residuary legislative power - Article 248, Part XI, Union List Entry 97

s: In which Part of the Constitution is the doctrine of repugnancy principally dealt with?
x: The doctrine of repugnancy is contained in Article 254, which is located in Part XI dealing with Union-State relations.
tq: Connect the doctrine's article with the constitutional Part containing legislative relations.
sec: Repugnancy - Article 254, President's assent exception

s: Under Article 254(1), when a State law and a Union law conflict on a Concurrent List subject, the normal consequence is that:
o: The Union law prevails and the State law is void to the extent of repugnancy
The State law prevails throughout India
The matter must be referred to the Governor
Both laws become void in their entirety
x: Article 254(1) gives predominance to the Union law in a Concurrent List conflict. The State law becomes void only to the extent of the repugnancy.
tq: Remember the limited effect of repugnancy: invalidity extends only to the conflicting portion.
sec: Repugnancy - Article 254, President's assent exception

s: A State law on a Concurrent List subject, reserved for the consideration of the President and receiving Presidential assent, will ordinarily:
o: Remain inoperative even within that State
Prevail in that State despite inconsistency with an earlier Union law
x: Under Article 254(2), such a State law prevails in the State concerned despite repugnancy with an earlier Union law. It does not prevail throughout India.
tq: Apply the Presidential-assent exception while limiting its territorial effect.
sec: Repugnancy - Article 254, President's assent exception

s: Which one of the following is a limitation on the protection given to a State law by Presidential assent under Article 254(2)?
o: Parliament may subsequently amend or repeal the State law by a fresh law.
The Supreme Court must approve the State law annually.
The Governor may never reserve the Bill again.
The State law automatically becomes part of the Union List.
x: Presidential assent gives the State law precedence in that State, but Parliament may later override it by amending or repealing it through a fresh law.
tq: Look for the later parliamentary override that qualifies the apparent State protection.
sec: Repugnancy - Article 254, President's assent exception

s: Which statement best describes the role of the Governor under Article 254(2)?
o: The Governor may repeal a Union law by executive order.
The Governor can declare a State law valid throughout India.
The Governor may reserve a Bill for the President as an exception to the usual aid-and-advice position.
The Governor must assent to every Bill involving repugnancy.
x: The Governor may reserve a State Bill for the President under Article 254(2), enabling the Presidential-assent exception to operate.
tq: Ask who performs the reservation step before the Presidential exception applies.
sec: Repugnancy - Article 254, President's assent exception

s: Parliamentary laws made under Articles 249 or 250 prevail over State laws under which provision?
x: Article 251 provides that laws made by Parliament under Articles 249 and 250 prevail over State laws. The State law becomes inoperative only while the Parliamentary law remains in force.
tq: Distinguish the special precedence rule in Article 251 from the general repugnancy rule in Article 254.
sec: Repugnancy - Article 254, President's assent exception

s: A State law made in a field covered by a Parliamentary law under Article 249 becomes inoperative:
o: Only after a declaration by the Supreme Court
Only while the Parliamentary law remains in force
Only when the State Legislature is dissolved
Permanently from the date of Presidential assent
x: Under Article 251, the State law is inoperative only for the duration of the Parliamentary law made under Article 249 or Article 250.
tq: Test the temporary nature of inoperability rather than treating it as permanent invalidity.
sec: Repugnancy - Article 254, President's assent exception

s:
Arrange the following in descending order of legislative predominance:
A. State List
B. Union List
C. Concurrent List
Select the correct sequence.
x: The order of predominance is Union List, followed by Concurrent List, followed by State List.
tq: Arrange the three Lists by constitutional predominance rather than by numerical order.
sec: Repugnancy - Article 254, President's assent exception

s: The doctrine of Pith and Substance requires a court primarily to examine:
o: The political party introducing the Bill
The title of the Act alone
The true object and character of the law, despite incidental encroachment on another field
Whether the law was passed unanimously
x: Under the doctrine of Pith and Substance, the court examines the true nature and object of the law. Incidental encroachment on another legislative field does not invalidate it.
tq: Apply the substance-over-form method to determine legislative competence.
sec: Repugnancy - Article 254, President's assent exception

s: Which of the following subjects was shifted from the State List to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976?
x: Education was one of the subjects transferred from the State List to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.
tq: Identify one transferred subject from the amendment's specific group.
sec: Repugnancy - Article 254, President's assent exception

s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with the subjects shifted to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment?
1. Forests
2. Weights and measures
3. Protection of wild animals and birds
4. Administration of justice, excluding the Supreme Court and High Courts
Select the correct answer using the code below.
x: All four subjects listed—forests, weights and measures, protection of wild animals and birds, and administration of justice excluding the Supreme Court and High Courts—were shifted to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment.
tq: Use the all-inclusive option after checking each item against the amendment group.
sec: Repugnancy - Article 254, President's assent exception

s: Which one of the following was NOT among the subjects shifted from the State List to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976?
o: Protection of wild animals and birds
x: Education, forests, and protection of wild animals and birds were shifted by the 42nd Amendment. Public health and sanitation was not among the five subjects specified.
tq: Find the nearby but excluded State List subject from the specified amendment group.
sec: Repugnancy - Article 254, President's assent exception

s: Which statement correctly identifies the constitutional exception to the normal rule of Union-law predominance under Article 254?
o: A State law on a Concurrent List matter always prevails if enacted later.
A State law reserved for and assented to by the President may prevail in that State.
A State law prevails whenever the Governor withholds assent.
A State law prevails if it concerns taxation alone.
x: Article 254(2) permits a State law on a Concurrent List subject to prevail in that State when it has been reserved for and assented to by the President, subject to later Parliamentary override.
tq: Locate the precise exception and reject broader versions of the rule.
sec: Repugnancy - Article 254, President's assent exception

s: Article 255 of the Constitution primarily relates to which of the following?
o: Repugnancy between Union and State laws
Recommendations and previous sanctions as matters of procedure
x: Article 255 provides that certain recommendations and previous sanctions are matters of procedure. Their absence does not necessarily invalidate an Act if the required assent is subsequently given.
tq: Use the article-number and subject association without confusing procedural requirements with substantive invalidity.
sec: Part XI Chapter I - Articles 245-255; Article 255  [APPSC]

s: Under Article 246A, Parliament and the State Legislatures have power to make laws relating to which subject?
x: Article 246A deals with the legislative power relating to Goods and Services Tax.
tq: Discriminate between closely placed Article 246 provisions and their distinct subjects.
sec: Part XI Chapter I - Articles 245-255; Article 255  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following is specifically authorised by Article 247?
o: The President may establish courts for State laws
The Governor may establish additional High Courts
The Supreme Court may create courts for local bodies
Parliament may establish additional courts for better administration of Union laws
x: Article 247 empowers Parliament to establish additional courts for the better administration of laws made by Parliament or existing laws relating to matters in the Union List.
tq: Ask who has the power and for what purpose; this avoids authority-swapping traps.
sec: Part XI Chapter I - Articles 245-255; Article 255  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 248 deals with residuary legislative powers.
2. Article 252 enables Parliament to legislate for two or more States with their consent.
3. States adopting a law under Article 252 cannot subsequently adopt it if they were not original consenting States.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. A State that did not originally consent may subsequently adopt the parliamentary law under Article 252; therefore, statement 3 is false.
tq: Find the incorrect absolute statement concerning later adoption by other States.
sec: Part XI Chapter I - Articles 245-255; Article 255  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following correctly describes the legislative effect of Article 253?
o: It applies only during a National Emergency
It permits States alone to implement international agreements
It permits Parliament to make laws implementing international agreements
It is confined to agreements concerning the Union List
x: Article 253 empowers Parliament to make laws for implementing treaties, agreements and conventions with foreign countries or decisions made at international conferences.
tq: Test the scope of parliamentary power by rejecting restrictive words such as 'only' and 'confined'.
sec: Part XI Chapter I - Articles 245-255; Article 255  [APPSC]

s: A law made by Parliament under Article 249 or Article 250 is inconsistent with a law made by a State Legislature. Which law prevails during the relevant period?
o: The law made later by the Governor
The State law, because State subjects are exclusively protected
x: Article 251 deals with inconsistency between laws made under Articles 249 or 250 and State laws. The Parliamentary law prevails to the extent of inconsistency.
tq: Link the operative article on inconsistency with the exceptional source of parliamentary power.
sec: Part XI Chapter I - Articles 245-255; Article 255  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following statements regarding Article 254 is correct?
o: A State law always prevails over a Union law in the Concurrent List
A Union law generally prevails over an inconsistent State law in the Concurrent field
Repugnancy applies only between Union List and State List laws
A State law assented to by the Chief Justice can prevail throughout India
x: Article 254 provides that Union law ordinarily prevails over an inconsistent State law in the Concurrent field. A State law reserved for and receiving the President's assent may prevail in that State.
tq: Use the field of operation and the assent exception to distinguish repugnancy from ordinary legislative conflict.
sec: Part XI Chapter I - Articles 245-255; Article 255  [APPSC]

s: An Act requiring the previous recommendation or sanction of the Governor or President has been passed without it, but the Governor or President subsequently gives assent. What is the constitutional consequence under Article 255?
o: The Act is not invalid merely for want of that recommendation or previous sanction
The Act is automatically void in all circumstances
The Act applies only to Union Territories
The Act becomes a constitutional amendment
x: Article 255 treats the requirement of recommendation or previous sanction as a matter of procedure. Subsequent assent prevents invalidity on that ground alone.
tq: Apply the procedural-versus-substantive distinction to a short constitutional situation.
sec: Part XI Chapter I - Articles 245-255; Article 255  [APPSC]

s:
Which of the following combinations is correctly matched?
1. Article 245 — Territorial extent of laws
2. Article 246 — Subject-matter of laws under the Seventh Schedule
3. Article 248 — Residuary powers
4. Article 255 — Repugnancy between Union and State laws
x: Articles 245, 246 and 248 are correctly matched. Repugnancy is dealt with by Article 254, not Article 255; Article 255 concerns recommendations and previous sanctions as procedural matters.
tq: Catch the swapped article number in an otherwise familiar constitutional sequence.
sec: Part XI Chapter I - Articles 245-255; Article 255  [APPSC]

s:
With reference to the territorial extent of laws, consider the following statements:
1. Parliament may make laws for the whole or any part of India.
2. Parliament's law is not invalid merely because it has extra-territorial operation.
3. A State Legislature may ordinarily legislate for the territory of another State without any territorial connection.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Parliament may legislate for the whole or any part of India, and an extra-territorial operation does not by itself invalidate parliamentary legislation. A State law requires a sufficient territorial nexus for extra-territorial reach, so statement 3 is false.
tq: Test the Union-State contrast and reject the unrestricted claim about State extra-territorial legislation.
sec: Territorial extent of laws - Article 245  [other exams]

s: Which constitutional authority's regulations have the force of Acts of Parliament in the Union Territories of Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep?
o: The Administrator appointed by the Supreme Court
x: Regulations made by the President for Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep have the force and effect of an Act of Parliament.
tq: Identify the competent authority instead of confusing Union Territory administration with State gubernatorial power.
sec: Territorial extent of laws - Article 245  [other exams]

s: Which of the following statements about legislative powers in specified tribal or Scheduled Areas is correct?
o: The Governor of every State may repeal any parliamentary Act throughout India
The President has no role in tribal areas of the North-Eastern States
Only the State Legislature may modify parliamentary Acts in Scheduled Areas
The Governor may bar or modify the application of parliamentary Acts in Scheduled Areas
x: The Governor may bar or modify the application of Acts of Parliament in Scheduled Areas. Special powers also exist for the Governor of Assam in Assam tribal areas and for the President in tribal areas of Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
tq: Use the territorial exception while rejecting overbroad claims about the Governor's power.
sec: Territorial extent of laws - Article 245  [other exams]

s: The doctrine of pith and substance is applied primarily to determine which of the following?
o: The true nature and character of a law when legislative fields overlap
The distribution of seats in the Rajya Sabha
The validity of a constitutional amendment under Article 368
x: Under the doctrine of pith and substance, the true object and character of a law determine the relevant legislative List. Incidental encroachment on another List is generally ignored.
tq: Match the doctrine with its precise constitutional problem rather than its incidental effect.
sec: Doctrine of pith and substance applied to list conflicts - cases

s: A State law on prohibition incidentally affects a matter in another legislative field, but its true nature is within the State List. Which case is associated with upholding such legislation under the doctrine of pith and substance?
o: State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee v. Bank of Commerce
K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa
x: In State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951), the prohibition law was upheld under the doctrine of pith and substance. The incidental encroachment did not alter its true character.
tq: Connect the factual subject of a case with the doctrine applied in that case.
sec: Doctrine of pith and substance applied to list conflicts - cases

s: Which one of the following expressions correctly represents the doctrine of colourable legislation?
o: The later law always overrides the earlier law
What cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly
A State law is valid only if Parliament approves it
Every law must be interpreted narrowly
x: The doctrine of colourable legislation is expressed by the maxim that what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. It is associated with K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa (1953).
tq: Test the exact maxim associated with a confusable constitutional doctrine.
sec: Doctrine of pith and substance applied to list conflicts - cases

s: Which doctrine requires legislative entries to be read together so that each can operate harmoniously?
x: Harmonious construction requires apparently overlapping entries to be interpreted together so that both retain operative effect.
tq: Discriminate among neighbouring doctrines by their operative principle.
sec: Doctrine of pith and substance applied to list conflicts - cases

s: Which one of the following sets contains only subjects in the Union List?
o: Defence, foreign affairs and atomic energy
Public order, local government and economic planning
x: Defence, foreign affairs and atomic energy are Union List subjects. Police, prisons, sports, public order and local government are State subjects, while education, forests, social security and economic planning are in the Concurrent List.
tq: Group subjects by List and eliminate sets containing a neighbouring-list item.
sec: Subject → list  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
x: Sports is a State List subject under Entry 33, not a Concurrent List subject. Prisons, local government and forests are correctly matched with their respective Lists and entries.
tq: Find the reversed List classification in a list-entry matching question.
sec: Subject → list  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Education is placed in the Concurrent List under Entry 25. It was transferred from the State List by which Constitutional Amendment?
x: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment transferred education from the State List to the Concurrent List, where it is covered by Entry 25.
tq: Combine the present List position with the amendment that changed it.
sec: Subject → list  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Social security and social insurance — Concurrent List, Entry 23
Economic and social planning — State List, Entry 20
x: Social security and social insurance are in the Concurrent List under Entry 23. Economic and social planning is Concurrent Entry 20, forests are Concurrent Entry 17A, and education is Concurrent Entry 25.
tq: Use the List and entry number together to expose deliberate classification swaps.
sec: Subject → list  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Coordination and determination of standards in institutions for higher education is covered by which entry?
x: Coordination and determination of standards in institutions for higher education is a Union List subject under Entry 66.
tq: Distinguish the Union entries concerning institutions of national importance and higher-education standards.
sec: Subject → list  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Which one of the following correctly identifies the entries relating to elections to State Legislatures and elections conducted by the Election Commission?
o: State Entry 37 and Union Entry 72 respectively
Union Entry 37 and State Entry 72 respectively
Concurrent Entry 25 and Union Entry 64 respectively
State Entry 50 and Concurrent Entry 20 respectively
x: Elections to the State Legislature are covered by State List Entry 37, subject to parliamentary law. Union Entry 72 covers elections conducted by the Election Commission.
tq: Separate the subject-specific State entry from the Union entry relating to Election Commission elections.
sec: Subject → list  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Which of the following is correctly matched with the State List?
x: Land is a State List subject under Entry 18. Atomic energy, organisation of High Courts and higher-education standards are Union List subjects under Entries 6, 78 and 66 respectively.
tq: Identify the State entry while eliminating familiar Union List entries.
sec: Subject → list  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Mineral rights taxation — State List Entry 50
x: Atomic energy is a Union List subject under Entry 6, not a State List subject. Public order, police and taxes on mineral rights are correctly associated with State List Entries 1, 2 and 50.
tq: Watch for a wrong List label attached to an otherwise correct entry number.
sec: Subject → list  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

s: A State Legislature passes a law whose true subject is within the State List, although the law incidentally affects a Union List matter. Which principle would most directly support its validity?
x: The doctrine of pith and substance looks to the true nature and character of the law and disregards incidental encroachment on another legislative field.
tq: Apply the doctrine to an overlap scenario by focusing on the law's true subject.
sec: Doctrine of pith and substance applied to list conflicts - cases

s: Under Article 252, a parliamentary law made on a State subject at the request of two or more States may subsequently be adopted by:
o: Only the States that originally requested it
The President without any State resolution
The Supreme Court through an advisory opinion
Any other State by passing a resolution in its Legislature
x: Article 252 permits Parliament to legislate for two or more consenting States on a State subject. Any other State may later adopt that law by passing a resolution in its Legislature.
tq: Test the consent mechanism and the route by which additional States may adopt the law.
sec: Part XI Chapter I - Articles 245-255; Article 255  [APPSC]

s: With respect to restrictions imposed by a State on inter-State trade, which one of the following is correct?
o: Every restriction is prohibited irrespective of public interest
Parliament can discriminate freely between States during normal conditions
Reasonable restrictions in the public interest may be imposed, but the Bill requires the President's previous sanction
The Governor's previous sanction is sufficient in every case
x: A State may impose reasonable restrictions on inter-State trade in the public interest, but a Bill for that purpose requires the President's previous sanction. Parliament is also restricted from discriminating between States except in situations of scarcity.
tq: Combine the substantive test of reasonableness with the procedural requirement of prior sanction.
sec: Part XI Chapter I - Articles 245-255; Article 255  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following statements regarding parliamentary legislation for implementing international agreements is correct?
o: Only the concerned State Legislature may implement such an agreement
Parliament may make a law for implementing an international treaty or agreement even when the subject would otherwise fall outside its ordinary legislative field
Parliament may legislate only if the subject is already in the Union List
Such legislation is possible only after a Rajya Sabha resolution under Article 249
x: Article 253 empowers Parliament to make laws for implementing international treaties, agreements and conventions, notwithstanding the ordinary distribution of legislative subjects.
tq: Reject restrictions imported from Article 249 and identify the independent treaty-implementation power.
sec: Part XI Chapter I - Articles 245-255; Article 255  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following is the odd one out with reference to the Concurrent List in the Seventh Schedule?
x: Fisheries is a State List subject. Succession, criminal law and civil procedure are subjects in the Concurrent List.
tq: Identify the subject belonging to a different list rather than relying on a familiar association.
sec: Odd one out - item not in a given list

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Trade and commerce within a State — Union List
x: Agriculture is a State List subject. Trade and commerce within a State, currency and foreign loans are not correctly placed in the alternatives given.
tq: Use the list allocation of familiar subjects to eliminate swapped entries.
sec: Odd one out - item not in a given list

s: The Seventh Schedule of the Constitution is primarily concerned with the distribution of legislative subjects among the Union, States and both. This scheme is contained in which Article?
x: Article 246 gives the constitutional framework for the distribution of legislative subjects in the three lists of the Seventh Schedule.
tq: Distinguish the article establishing the legislative distribution from articles dealing with special powers.
sec: Seventh Schedule - three lists, entries originally and now

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The scheme of legislative distribution in India was borrowed from the Canadian model.
2. The Concurrent List has roots in the Government of India Act, 1935.
3. The Indian Constitution contains only two legislative lists.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the Seventh Schedule contains Union, State and Concurrent Lists.
tq: Reject the extreme numerical statement after confirming the two historically correct statements.
sec: Seventh Schedule - three lists, entries originally and now

s: Which of the following correctly represents the usual order of predominance among the three legislative lists?
o: State List > Concurrent List > Union List
Union List > State List > Concurrent List
Union List > Concurrent List > State List
Concurrent List > Union List > State List
x: The Union List has the greatest predominance, followed by the Concurrent List and then the State List.
tq: Test the relative hierarchy rather than memorising the lists in isolation.
sec: Seventh Schedule - three lists, entries originally and now

s:
Which of the following were transferred from the State List to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment?
1. Education
2. Forests
3. Weights and measures
4. Administration of justice and organisation of courts other than the Supreme Court and High Courts
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: All four listed subjects were shifted by the 42nd Amendment. The judicial entry excludes the Supreme Court and High Courts.
tq: Check the complete list and pay attention to the qualification attached to courts.
sec: Entries shifted by the 42nd Amendment (1976)

s: Entry 92A, relating to inter-State sales tax, was added to the Union List by which Constitutional Amendment?
x: The Sixth Amendment Act, 1956 added Entry 92A concerning inter-State sales tax to the Union List.
tq: Match the specific entry with its amendment year while avoiding the nearby Seventh and Forty-second Amendments.
sec: Entries shifted by the 42nd Amendment (1976)

s: The constitutional basis for Parliament enacting the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act is primarily found in which entry?
x: Prevention of cruelty to animals is placed in Concurrent List Entry 17, enabling Parliament to enact central legislation on the subject.
tq: Distinguish the Concurrent List entry on animal cruelty from the State entry on preservation of livestock.
sec: Constitutional basis for central laws on unusual subjects

s:
With reference to cow slaughter, consider the following statements:
1. Preservation of livestock is a State List subject.
2. Article 48 is relevant to the constitutional policy concerning preservation of livestock.
3. Parliament may legislate on the subject only through the ordinary Union List power.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false: Parliament can legislate on the State subject through Articles 249, 250 or 252, among the specified routes.
tq: Spot the wrong statement that incorrectly converts a special legislative route into an ordinary Union power.
sec: Constitutional basis for central laws on unusual subjects

s:
Article 253 empowers Parliament to make laws for implementing which of the following?
1. Treaties
2. International agreements and conventions
3. Decisions of international bodies
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: Article 253 covers treaties, international agreements, conventions and decisions of international bodies. Such legislation may extend to State List subjects and does not require State consent.
tq: Select the comprehensive option after checking each constitutional trigger separately.
sec: Constitutional basis for central laws on unusual subjects

s: A law is required to implement an international environmental convention, although the subject otherwise falls in the State List. Which constitutional provision directly supports Parliament's competence?
x: Article 253 authorises Parliament to legislate for implementing treaties, agreements, conventions and decisions of international bodies, even on State List subjects.
tq: Identify the constitutional route from the purpose of the legislation rather than from the subject alone.
sec: Constitutional basis for central laws on unusual subjects

s: Which one of the following is NOT a constitutional limitation on Parliament's legislative power?
o: The requirement that every Parliamentary law must receive prior consent of all State Legislatures
The federal division of legislative subjects
x: Prior consent of all State Legislatures is not a general requirement. Parliament is limited by the written Constitution, Fundamental Rights, the federal allocation of powers and the Basic Structure.
tq: Reject the overbroad consent requirement and retain the actual constitutional limitations.
sec: Limits on Parliament's legislative competence

s:
Which of the following Articles provides special routes through which Parliament may legislate on State List matters?
1. Article 249
2. Article 250
3. Article 252
4. Article 253
5. Article 356
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: Articles 249, 250, 252, 253 and 356 are the stated constitutional routes permitting Parliament to legislate in fields otherwise within the State List.
tq: Build the answer by checking every listed exception to the normal federal allocation.
sec: Limits on Parliament's legislative competence

s: Parliament enacts a law having operation outside the territory of India. Which statement is constitutionally correct?
o: Such operation is valid only after approval by every State Legislature.
Such operation is permitted only during a Proclamation of Emergency.
Such operation is permitted under Article 245(2).
Such operation is always invalid because Parliament has no extra-territorial competence.
x: Article 245(2) protects Parliamentary laws from invalidity merely because they have extra-territorial operation.
tq: Use the constitutional exception to avoid treating territorial limits as absolute.
sec: Limits on Parliament's legislative competence

s: Articles 301 to 303 principally restrict Parliament from doing which of the following in relation to trade and commerce?
o: Making any law concerning inter-State trade
x: Articles 301 to 303 restrict discriminatory or preferential treatment between States in laws relating to trade and commerce.
tq: Distinguish a restriction against discrimination from a complete prohibition on regulation.
sec: Limits on Parliament's legislative competence

s: In India, the residuary power of legislation is vested in Parliament by which combination?
o: Article 248 and Entry 97 of the Union List
Article 249 and Entry 97 of the State List
Article 250 and Entry 98 of the Concurrent List
Article 253 and Entry 97 of the Concurrent List
x: Article 248 and Entry 97 of the Union List together confer residuary legislative power on Parliament.
tq: Link the constitutional article with the corresponding Seventh Schedule entry.
sec: Residuary powers compared with USA, Canada, Australia

s: Which description best explains the comparative basis of India's residuary arrangement?
o: It follows the American and Australian model of vesting residue in the States.
It follows the Canadian model of vesting residue in the Centre and reflects a strong Centre.
It leaves residuary matters exclusively to the Concurrent List.
It follows a purely confederal model in which residue is jointly exercised.
x: India follows the Canadian approach by placing residuary powers with the Centre, contributing to a comparatively strong Union.
tq: Use the comparative model to distinguish Canada from the USA and Australia.
sec: Universal angles

s: Which one of the following statements regarding Article 252 is correct?
o: A law made under Article 252 cannot be changed by State Legislatures.
Article 252 requires no legislative action by Parliament.
Article 252 applies only to Union List subjects.
A law made under Article 252 can be amended or repealed by any one State Legislature unilaterally.
x: Parliamentary legislation made under Article 252 on the request of States cannot be altered unilaterally by State Legislatures.
tq: Test the legal consequence of a special legislative route rather than its general subject matter.
sec: Universal angles

s: Which of the following examples has been cited in debates concerning use of the Concurrent List to reach State subjects?
o: Farm Laws through Concurrent List Entry 33
Currency regulation through State List Entry 15
Foreign affairs through Concurrent List Entry 3
x: Farm Laws were discussed as an example of Concurrent List Entry 33 being used in a field associated with agriculture, which is State List Entry 14.
tq: Match the debated law with the relevant Concurrent List entry and the associated State subject.
sec: Universal angles

s:
Consider the following statements regarding centralising pressures in India's federal structure:
1. The Concurrent List has been criticised as a route for Union encroachment into State subjects.
2. The NEP and the NMC Act have been cited in this debate.
3. Article 254(2) and Articles 249 and 252 have also been discussed as centralising tools.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All three statements reflect the cited debate concerning the Union's use of concurrent and exceptional legislative powers.
tq: Confirm the common theme across examples, then select the complete combination.
sec: Universal angles

s: The Supreme Court's advisory opinion of November 2025 was reported in connection with which issue?
o: Deemed assent and timelines for Governors and the President
Allocation of residuary powers to States
Transfer of forests to the Union List
x: The advisory opinion rejected deemed assent and fixed timelines concerning Governors and the President.
tq: Identify the constitutional controversy from the paired concepts rather than from a general federalism label.
sec: Universal angles

s: The MMDR (Amendment) Bill, 2026 was reported as restricting the States' power to tax which subject?
x: The Bill was reported as restricting State taxation power over mineral rights and mineral-bearing land. Kerala viewed this as encroachment on State List Entries 18 and 50.
tq: Match the legislative development with the precise fiscal subject affected.
sec: Universal angles

s: Which State was reported as objecting to the MMDR (Amendment) Bill, 2026 on the ground that it encroached upon State Entries 18 and 50?
x: Kerala criticised the measure as an encroachment on State powers relating to Entries 18 and 50 and indicated that it might approach the courts.
tq: Use the named State and entry numbers as a precise current-affairs combination.
sec: Universal angles

s:
With reference to preventive detention, consider the following statements:
1. Union List Entry 9 covers defence, foreign affairs and security.
2. Concurrent List Entry 3 covers State security and public order.
3. Preventive detention is placed exclusively in the State List.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct because preventive detention-related powers are divided between Union List Entry 9 and Concurrent List Entry 3. Statement 3 is false because the subject is not exclusively in the State List.
tq: Reject the exclusive-allocation trap when the constitutional scheme divides a subject between lists.
sec: Universal angles

s: The Allahabad High Court's criticism of routine preventive detention was discussed in the context of which legislative distribution?
o: Preventive detention powers being divided between Union List Entry 9 and Concurrent List Entry 3
Preventive detention being solely a State List matter
Preventive detention being governed only by Article 253
Preventive detention being solely a Union List matter
x: The relevant distribution divides the subject between Union List Entry 9, dealing with defence, foreign affairs and security, and Concurrent List Entry 3, dealing with State security and public order.
tq: Apply the list entries to the institutional controversy instead of choosing an exclusive category.
sec: Universal angles
